extracted.subtask_short: writing dialogue and setting in fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting believable dialogue (including exposition, dialect, profanity, and speech peculiarities) and for creating effective setting (place, time, mood, details, authenticity, and how setting interacts with character and plot).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid forced exposition in dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't have characters tell each other facts they already know just to convey exposition to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If exposition sounds forced or unrealistic, either rework the dialogue so the speaker has a plausible reason to introduce the information (example: make the speaker make a point that naturally includes the fact), or move the exposition into narration: e.g., instead of 'Troy, you were six years old when your mother left you...' revise to a line that uses the fact to make a point, or write 'At the age of six, Troy and his sister had the misfortune to be abandoned...' if no plausible dialogue reason exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make any dialogue exposition motivated and credible
rubrics_metrics.description: When information must appear in dialogue, it should serve a credible dramatic purpose for the speaker (e.g., to make a point, persuade, comfort, accuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: change a bare recitation of fact into a line that advances the speaker's intent ('Troy, grow up... Don't you think it's time you let go?') so the exposition doubles as character intention and avoids sounding like an authorial info-dump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't use dialogue as a platform for the author's views
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid making characters simply recite the writer's opinions or political arguments at length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long didactic speeches by characters risk making the reader feel manipulated and bored. While some authors (e.g., Ayn Rand, Sartre, Orwell) have successfully used this technique, it is extremely hard to pull off. If you want to argue a position, consider writing an essay or letter to the editor rather than forcing a fictional character to harangue another character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use profanity sparingly in written dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Written profanity reads as more alarming and vulgar than spoken profanity and often feels overused on the page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a couple of well-chosen swear words to a long string of expletives; select words that bring flavor without overwhelming the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tread carefully with dialect; less is more
rubrics_metrics.description: Heavy, phonetic, or exhaustive dialect risks sounding hackneyed, exaggerated, or offensive; aim to give only the flavor of a dialect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capture dialect through key words, characteristic speech patterns, and rhythms rather than attempting to phonetically transcribe every line. Example contrast: avoid overwhelming Yiddishisms ('Bubbela, the scare you gave me') and instead use a small number of touches that convey ethnicity without shoving it in the reader's face. Look to authors like Toni Morrison for models of subtle dialect use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative to heavy dialect: indicate accent and write normally
rubrics_metrics.description: You can communicate that a character has an accent or dialect without rendering all speech phonetically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have another character remark on the accent, or state that a character speaks with an accent, then write the dialogue in standard spelling—this avoids confusing the reader while making the point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't reproduce speech impediments in distracting, literal fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Showing stutters or other disfluencies by literal letter-by-letter reproduction can be distracting and hard to read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer simple attribution ('I'm not sure,' Joe stammered.) rather than 'I—I—I'm not sh-sure.' Be sparing with filler words ('uhm', 'uh', 'well', 'you know') so the dialogue flows and remains readable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground the reader in place with specific spatial details
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the reader clear indications of where characters are on multiple scales (planet, country, city, neighborhood, street, room).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sensory and specific description to paint place—examples given range from open prairie to Bronx underpass to Dublin Bay to luxurious Gatsby rooms. Provide enough detail to make the setting unmistakable without stopping the story's forward movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use weather as a tool to deepen the sense of place
rubrics_metrics.description: Weather can immediately deepen the visceral sensation of 'being' in a place and affect mood and character behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include sunny languor (Joyce Carol Oates) or snowstorms (Tolstoy). Consider how local weather patterns shape daily life and incorporate that where relevant (author notes Seattle's rain as formative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make place affect the action and plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The setting should have a causal or constraining relationship to what happens in the story—what's possible or normal in one place/time may be impossible in another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If place has no effect on the plot, look for ways to make it relevant; examples: All the Pretty Horses depends on the Southwest borderlands; Flannery O'Connor's road-setting precipitates the story's catastrophe. If the setting doesn't influence the story, characters may seem to drift through a vacuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locate characters in time (era, season, time of day)
rubrics_metrics.description: Always give readers orientation in time—both the large (era, year) and the small (season, day, hour).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time affects travel, clothing, social norms, and the story's possibilities (examples: Dickens vs. Thom Jones; spring vs. autumn vs. night in Salinger). Provide whatever temporal clues readers need to stay oriented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting to shape mood and emotional landscape
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond physical grounding, setting can evoke atmosphere and emotional states that support the drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poe's 'dull, dark, and soundless day' is an example of setting creating bleakness and danger; Lorrie Moore's hospital details make the setting nightmarish to her protagonist. Convey setting through the POV character's consciousness when appropriate so mood and perception align.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed setting into the action; avoid long descriptive 'globs'
rubrics_metrics.description: Scatter setting description throughout the piece and mix it with action rather than pausing the story for long, static paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep description concise and woven into what characters do (example: Marguerite Duras integrates setting by relating an anecdote tied to character action). Don't let setting descriptions halt narrative momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use telling details to convey setting efficiently
rubrics_metrics.description: A small, well-chosen detail can evoke an entire environment and make a scene feel lived-in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Russo's focus on an antiquated Hobart dishwasher conveys the diner vividly without listing every shabby detail. Choose sensory, specific items that carry associative weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust amount of setting description to its importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide how much 'space' to spend on a setting based on how central it is to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story unfolds entirely in one place (e.g., 'The Fall of the House of Usher'), more description is warranted. If a setting is incidental (a drugstore stop), brief mention suffices. Minimalism (e.g., Raymond Carver) can work when justified by POV or story needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for authenticity in setting; research or fictionalize
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray real or seemingly real settings accurately; if you don't know a place well, research it or give it a fictional name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visits or research (including the Internet) to verify details. If unsure, fictionalize (e.g., 'Leveland') to avoid errors or offending residents and to retain dramatic license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let setting shape character behavior and identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be influenced by their environment—how they dress, talk, socialize, work, and react.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characters can be plopped into any environment with no notable change, the setting isn't integrated. Seek subtle ways setting has seeped into a character rather than forcing stereotypes. Use fish-out-of-water scenarios to create conflict and reveal character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider making setting function as a character
rubrics_metrics.description: When a setting is overwhelmingly important, it can act and change, recurring as a dominant, evolving presence in the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the sea/waves in Virginia Woolf's The Waves, the moors in Wuthering Heights, or an era (Jazz Age) functioning as a character. When appropriate, let recurring images or changing landscapes unify and add meaning to the narrative.
